Whether it's a hospital nurse watching over a critically ill patient, a historical children's nurse raising a baby, or a worker bee feeding larvae, the word always carries this core idea of devoted, attentive, and skilled caregiving.

MeaningWho/WhatContext

In short: in everyday modern usage, a nurse is a licensed, trained medical professional who cares for sick and injured people. In older or specialized contexts, the word can also mean a caretaker of young children, a woman who breastfeeds another's baby, or a worker insect that tends the colony's young. All of these meanings share the same heart: someone dedicated to caring for those who need it most.
11189: Before diving into the individual meanings, it helps to know the single idea that connects all of them. When you nurse something, you give it careful, gentle, sustained attention — because that thing is either fragile, precious, wounded, or needs time to develop. Hold that idea in your mind, and every meaning below will feel natural.

1. To Feed a Baby from the Breast

This is the most literal meaning. When a mother nurses her baby, she feeds it milk directly from her breast. The baby is held close, kept warm, and nourished.

"She sat quietly and nursed her newborn."

You might also see it used the other way — the baby is said to be nursing.

"The baby was nursing contentedly."

2. To Care for a Sick or Injured Person

This is probably the most widely used meaning. To nurse someone means to look after them with close, continuous care — giving them medicine, keeping them comfortable, watching over their condition, and helping them recover.

"She nursed her father through a long illness."
"He was nursed back to health by the doctors and staff."

Notice the phrase "nursed back to health" — it's a very common expression. It means someone was so sick or hurt that they needed dedicated care to recover, and they received it.

This meaning is where the word nurse (the person, the noun) comes from — a nurse is someone whose job is to do exactly this.

3. To Take Care of Your Own Injury or Illness

You can also nurse yourself. When you are sick or hurt and you're carefully resting, keeping warm, taking medicine, and generally tending to your own body, you are nursing yourself.

"She stayed home and nursed her cold all weekend."
"He spent the evening nursing his sprained ankle with ice packs."

The key feeling here is deliberate, gentle self-care — not ignoring the problem, but attending to it steadily.

4. To Hold Something Gently and Carefully

To nurse an object means to hold it delicately, often cradling it in your hands, treating it as if it could be harmed or spilled.

"She nursed a hot cup of tea in both hands."
"He nursed the fragile antique vase as he carried it across the room."

The image here is gentle, protective physical contact — the way you might hold something you really don't want to drop or damage.

5. To Make Something Last by Using It Slowly and Carefully

This meaning is about conservation. When you nurse a limited resource — a drink, fuel, money, a battery — you use it very slowly and sparingly so it lasts as long as possible.

"He nursed his one glass of wine throughout the entire four-hour dinner."
"She was running low on fuel, so she nursed the car along the highway at a slow, steady speed."
"They had very little money left, so they nursed their savings through the final weeks of the trip."

The idea is that the thing is precious or limited, and you're being extremely careful not to waste it. You give it your constant, measured attention.

6. To Keep a Feeling Alive Inside You Over a Long Time

This is a powerful and very common meaning. You can nurse a feeling — an emotion, a wish, a belief, a resentment — by holding onto it quietly and privately, keeping it alive in your heart over a long period of time.

The feelings that are most often "nursed" tend to be ones that people hold privately and let grow slowly:

  • A grudge — a feeling of anger or resentment toward someone
  • A grievance — a sense that you were wronged
  • Ambitions or hopes — quiet, private desires for the future
  • A dream — a long-held wish

"For twenty years, he nursed a deep grudge against his former business partner."
"She had nursed the ambition to become a writer since she was a child."
"He nursed the hope that she would one day return."

The word choice of "nurse" here is very deliberate and meaningful. It suggests the feeling didn't explode suddenly — instead, the person tended to it, fed it, kept it alive through time, the way you would nurse a sick person. It's quiet, private, and persistent.

7. To Help Something Develop or Grow with Careful Attention

To nurse something along means to guide it through its early, fragile stage — giving it constant care and attention so that it survives and eventually grows strong.

"She nursed the struggling plant back to life with daily watering and care."
"He nursed the small startup company into a thriving business over ten years."
"The coach nursed the young player's talent carefully, never pushing him too hard too soon."

This is different from simply "helping" something. Nursing implies the thing was fragile, needed steady and patient attention, and might have failed without that careful guidance.

Here is the beautiful truth about this word: all seven meanings share the same soul.

Whether you are:

  • feeding a baby,
  • caring for a sick person,
  • cradling a cup of tea,
  • making your last bit of petrol last,
  • quietly holding onto a lifelong dream, or
  • slowly building a business from nothing —

...you are doing the same fundamental thing: giving something fragile or precious your careful, steady, gentle, and sustained attention.

That is what it means to nurse.
Quick Reference: The Pattern of Use

The verb "nurse" almost always appears in one of these structures:

  • nurse + someone → She nursed her mother through the illness.
  • nurse + something → He nursed a drink / a grudge / a hope / a cold.
  • nurse + someone/something + back to health / into something → She nursed the business into a success.
  • nurse + yourself → He stayed home and nursed himself.

Once you see the connecting thread — careful, gentle, sustained attention to something fragile or precious — this word becomes almost impossible to forget or misuse.
11190: Before diving into the individual meanings, here is something that ties them all together. A nursery is always a place specifically set aside for caring for, growing, or developing something young — whether that is a baby, a young child, a young plant, or a young animal. Once you hold onto that idea, every meaning of this word will make perfect sense.
Meaning 1: A Room in a Home for a Baby or Young Child

This is the most personal and everyday meaning. In a house or an apartment, a nursery is a dedicated room for a baby or a very young child. It is a space designed entirely around the child's needs — sleeping, feeding, and playing.

A nursery typically contains things like a crib or a small bed, a changing table, soft toys, and gentle lighting. The whole point of this room is to be a safe, comfortable, specially prepared space where a young child is looked after. Parents "set up the nursery" before a baby is born, meaning they prepare and decorate this special room.

Example: "They painted the nursery yellow and set up the crib near the window."
Meaning 2: A School for Very Young Children

A nursery (also called a nursery school) is an educational setting for very young children, typically between the ages of 2 and 5, before they are old enough to attend primary school.

In a nursery school, children are not learning to read textbooks or do complex maths. Instead, they learn through play, songs, stories, and social interaction. They develop basic skills like how to share, how to hold a pencil, how to communicate with others, and how to follow simple instructions. The focus is on nurturing the whole child — emotionally, socially, and intellectually — at a very early, sensitive stage of life.

Example: "She dropped her son off at nursery every morning before going to work."

Note: In British English, "nursery" is commonly used as a short form of "nursery school." In American English, people more often say "preschool" or "daycare," though "nursery" is still understood.
Meaning 3: A Place Where Plants Are Grown and Sold

This meaning might surprise you if you only knew the first one, but it makes perfect sense once you think about it. A plant nursery (or simply a "nursery") is a commercial place — like a farm or a garden centre — where plants are cultivated from seeds or cuttings, raised until they are healthy and strong, and then sold to customers.

A plant nursery might grow flowers, trees, shrubs, vegetable seedlings, or herbs. Just like a nursery school cares for young children until they are ready for the wider world, a plant nursery cares for young plants until they are strong enough to be planted in someone's garden.

When you buy a rose bush, a fruit tree, or a tray of tomato seedlings from a shop, there is a very good chance it was grown in a nursery before it reached you.

Example: "We went to the nursery to buy some lavender and a young apple tree for the garden."
Meaning 4: A Place Where Young Animals or Fish Are Raised

Less commonly, the word nursery is used for a place where young animals — especially fish — are raised in a controlled environment. Fish nurseries, for example, raise young fish (called fry or fingerlings) from eggs until they are big and strong enough to be released into rivers or oceans, or sold to fish farms.

In wildlife and nature contexts, you might also hear phrases like "nursery habitat" or "nursery ground" — meaning an area of the natural world (like a sheltered bay or a coral reef) where young animals tend to gather because they are protected and have plenty of food. The ocean acts as a nursery for countless species of marine life.

Example: "The shallow coastal waters serve as a nursery for young fish and shellfish."
Meaning 5: Figurative Use — Any Place That Develops or Produces Something

Because a nursery is fundamentally a place that fosters growth and development, the word is also used figuratively to describe any environment, institution, or situation that produces or develops a particular quality, skill, or type of person in large numbers.

Example: "The university has long been a nursery of political talent." (Meaning: the university has produced many talented politicians over the years.)

Example: "The streets of New Orleans were a nursery for jazz music." (Meaning: that environment gave birth to and nurtured the early development of jazz.)

This usage simply extends the core idea: something young and valuable is being carefully cultivated in a particular environment.

The word "nursery" appears in several fixed phrases that are very commonly used:

  • Nursery rhyme: A short, simple poem or song that has been traditionally sung or recited to young children. Examples include "Humpty Dumpty" and "Baa Baa Black Sheep." They are called nursery rhymes because they were originally recited in the nursery — the room where children were kept and cared for.
  • Nursery school: A formal school for children aged roughly 2–5, as explained in Meaning 2 above.
  • Nursery slope (or nursery run): In skiing, this refers to a gentle, easy slope designated for complete beginners — usually children — who are just learning to ski. The slope "nurses" them into the sport safely, before they move on to steeper terrain.
  • Nursery stakes / nursery race: In horse racing, a race specifically for young horses (two-year-olds). Same logic — it is a competition for animals still in their early developmental stage.

If it's about…Think of "nursery" as…

No matter which context you encounter "nursery" in, ask yourself: Is this a place where something young is being carefully cared for and developed? If the answer is yes, you are looking at a nursery.

A baby's room → yes. A preschool → yes. A plant shop → yes. A fish-rearing facility → yes. A city that produced generations of great artists → yes, figuratively.

That single thread — a place dedicated to nurturing something young — runs through every single use of this word.
11191:
Nurturance is the warm, caring support that a person gives to someone else to help them grow, feel safe, and thrive — emotionally, mentally, and physically.

Think of it this way: when a parent holds a crying child, soothes them, feeds them, encourages them, and makes them feel loved and secure — all of that, taken together, is nurturance. It is not just one action. It is the whole generous spirit of caring for another person's well-being and development.

The word comes from the idea of nurturing, which most people already understand. But nurturance as a noun names that quality as a thing in itself — like a force, a trait, or a practice that someone carries and gives.

It has two sides:

1. The giving side — the care, attention, warmth, and support that one person actively provides to another.

2. The receiving side — what the other person takes in and benefits from.

Both sides matter when you use this word.

Nurturance is not just feeding someone or keeping them physically safe. It covers a much richer range of things:

  • Emotional warmth — making someone feel loved, valued, and accepted.
  • Responsiveness — noticing when someone needs help and actually responding to that need, rather than ignoring it.
  • Encouragement — supporting someone's growth, confidence, and abilities.
  • Protection — creating a safe environment where a person feels secure enough to develop.
  • Consistency — being reliably present and caring, not just occasionally.
  • Sensitivity — understanding and responding to the other person's feelings and needs with gentleness.

All of these together form what we call nurturance.
Who Gives It, and Who Receives It?

Most commonly, nurturance is talked about in the context of parents and children. A mother comforting her scared child, a father teaching his son to ride a bike with patience and encouragement — these are classic examples of nurturance in action.

But it is not limited to parenting. Nurturance can flow between:

  • A teacher and a student
  • A therapist and a client
  • A caregiver and an elderly person
  • Friends supporting each other through hard times
  • Partners in a close relationship

In fact, psychologists recognize that adults need nurturance too — not just children. The need to feel cared for, supported, and emotionally tended to is a basic human need throughout life.

In psychology, nurturance is also used to describe a trait — a stable tendency or drive that some people have more strongly than others.

A person with high nurturance is someone who:

  • Genuinely enjoys caring for others
  • Feels drawn to help, comfort, and support people around them
  • Is warm, attentive, and emotionally generous by nature

This use of the word shifts slightly — instead of describing an act of care, it describes a person's inner disposition to give care. You might say a nurse, a devoted parent, or a compassionate friend has a high degree of nurturance.

Conversely, psychologists also speak of a person's need for nurturance — meaning how much a person craves being cared for, supported, and loved by others. Someone who grew up without enough emotional care, for example, may have a strong unmet need for nurturance.

It helps to separate nurturance from things that sound similar:

  • It is not the same as love alone. Love is a feeling. Nurturance is active — it is love expressed through consistent care and supportive action.
  • It is not the same as discipline or teaching, though those can sometimes coexist with it. Nurturance is specifically about warmth, support, and emotional care.
  • It is not smothering or overprotection. True nurturance supports growth and independence — it does not control or hold back.
  • It is not pity. Nurturance comes from a place of warmth and respect, not from looking down on someone as helpless.

Research in psychology and child development consistently shows that nurturance is one of the most important things a child needs to grow into a healthy, secure, and emotionally stable adult. Children who receive high nurturance tend to develop better self-esteem, stronger social skills, and greater resilience in the face of difficulty.

Even in adulthood, relationships high in nurturance — where partners, friends, or colleagues genuinely support each other's well-being — are linked to better mental health, lower stress, and greater life satisfaction.

In short, nurturance is not a soft or trivial concept. It is a cornerstone of human development and emotional well-being at every stage of life.
One Final Way to Remember It

If you want a simple mental anchor for this word:

Nurturance = the steady, warm, active care that helps a living being grow and flourish.

It is the soil, the sunlight, and the water — not just for plants, but for people.
11192:
To nurture something means to care for it consistently and lovingly over time so that it can grow, develop, and become the best version of itself. It is not a single action you do once. It is a continuous, devoted process of giving something — or someone — what it needs to flourish.

Think of a gardener and a seed. The gardener doesn't just plant the seed and walk away. They water it regularly, make sure it gets sunlight, protect it from harsh weather, and remove weeds that might choke it. That entire, ongoing effort of careful, loving attention is what it means to nurture something.

Many words involve caring for something. You can feed a child, protect a child, or teach a child. But to nurture a child means all of that and more — it captures the whole spirit of devoted, patient, thoughtful care that is aimed at helping someone grow into their full potential.

The word carries warmth. It implies that the person doing the nurturing genuinely cares. There is love, patience, and dedication built into the word. You cannot nurture something carelessly or in a hurry. Nurturing is slow, attentive, and deeply personal.

This is where the word becomes really rich and useful, because you can nurture both living things and abstract things.

People and living things. A mother nurtures her child by providing food, comfort, emotional support, encouragement, and guidance through every stage of life. A teacher nurtures students by recognising their individual strengths and helping each one grow. A farmer nurtures crops by giving them the right soil, water, and care they need to yield a good harvest.

Talents and skills. You can nurture a gift or an ability. If someone says, "She nurtured her talent for music from a very young age," it means she consistently practiced, studied, and devoted herself to developing that talent over many years until it grew into something remarkable. The talent did not just appear fully formed — it was carefully tended to.

Ideas and creativity. You can nurture an idea, a project, or a creative work. A writer might nurture a story for years — revisiting it, refining it, adding to it — before it is ready to be shared with the world. A scientist nurtures a hypothesis by gathering evidence, testing it, and gradually building it into a solid theory.

Relationships. Friendships, marriages, and professional partnerships all need to be nurtured. If you neglect a relationship, it weakens. If you nurture it — through regular communication, honesty, support, and kindness — it grows stronger and deeper over time.

Feelings, values, and hopes. You can nurture confidence in a shy child by regularly praising their efforts and encouraging them to try new things. A community can nurture a sense of belonging by making everyone feel included and valued. Parents nurture values like honesty or kindness in their children by modelling those values themselves and gently reinforcing them over time.

No matter what is being nurtured, two things are always present in the meaning of the word.

The first is care — genuine, attentive, thoughtful care. You are not neglecting the thing. You are actively paying attention to what it needs and providing it.

The second is growth as the goal — you are not just keeping something alive or maintaining the status quo. You are helping it develop, improve, and reach a higher or fuller state. A plant you nurture doesn't just survive; it thrives. A child you nurture doesn't just grow up; they grow up well.

It helps to understand what nurturing is not, so you can see its edges clearly.

Nurturing is not controlling. When you nurture something, you are serving its needs and its potential, not imposing your own will on it. A parent who forces a child into a career the child hates is not nurturing them — they are controlling them.

Nurturing is not instant. You cannot nurture something overnight. If someone says they "nurtured" a business from a small startup to a successful company, you immediately understand that this took years of steady effort and care.

Nurturing is not passive. It is not simply leaving something alone and hoping it turns out fine. It requires active, ongoing involvement and attention.

When you read or hear the word "nurture," it creates a feeling of warmth, gentleness, and hope. It suggests that something is being looked after by someone who truly cares, and that something good is growing as a result. It is one of those words that carries an entire emotional attitude inside it — the attitude of a devoted caregiver who believes in the potential of what they are tending to.

"She worked hard to nurture her students' curiosity, encouraging them to ask questions and explore ideas freely."

"The company nurtured a culture of trust by being transparent with its employees and valuing their input."

"He had always nurtured a dream of becoming a writer, filling notebook after notebook with stories since childhood."

"Good leaders nurture the people around them, helping them grow into their own leadership potential."

"The mentorship programme was designed to nurture young scientists from underrepresented communities."
The One-Sentence Definition You Can Always Return To

If you ever need to recall this word quickly, remember this: to nurture something is to care for it with consistent love and attention so that it can grow and reach its potential. Everything else — the warmth, the patience, the long-term commitment, the range of things that can be nurtured — flows naturally from that core idea.
11193: The word nutmeg has a few distinct meanings depending on the context you encounter it in. Here is each one explained fully.

Nutmeg is a spice — a flavoring used in cooking and food preparation. It comes in two forms:

  • Whole nutmeg: a hard, oval-shaped seed, roughly the size of an apricot pit, with a rough brownish surface.
  • Ground nutmeg: a fine, light-brown powder made by grating or grinding that seed.

The flavor of nutmeg is warm, sweet, slightly spicy, and woody — somewhat like a mix of cinnamon and pepper but softer and more complex. The smell is equally distinctive: rich, aromatic, and a little earthy. Even a small amount of nutmeg can dramatically change the character of a dish, which is why recipes typically call for just a pinch or a tiny grating.

Where does it come from?

Nutmeg comes from the nutmeg tree, an evergreen tropical tree that originally grew only on the Banda Islands in Indonesia. Today it is cultivated in Indonesia, Grenada (which is one of the world's leading producers and even features nutmeg on its national flag), India, Sri Lanka, and other tropical regions.

The tree produces a fleshy yellow fruit that looks somewhat like a peach. When the fruit ripens and splits open, it reveals the seed inside — that seed is the nutmeg. Surrounding the seed, you will notice a bright red, lacy, web-like covering called an aril. That red covering is dried and sold as a completely separate spice called mace, which has a similar but more delicate flavor than nutmeg.

So from one fruit, you get two spices: nutmeg (the seed) and mace (the covering of the seed).

How is nutmeg used in cooking?

Nutmeg is incredibly versatile. It shows up in:

  • Sweet dishes: custards, rice pudding, eggnog, pumpkin pie, fruit cakes, biscuits, and other baked goods.
  • Savory dishes: béchamel sauce (the classic white sauce used in lasagna and pasta), creamed spinach, meat dishes, sausages, and soups.
  • Drinks: mulled wine, chai tea, and warm spiced milk.
  • South Asian and Middle Eastern cooking: biryanis, curries, and spiced rice dishes often use nutmeg.

When used in cooking, nutmeg is usually added in very small quantities — a tiny pinch of the ground spice, or a few passes of a whole nutmeg over a fine grater. Many cooks prefer grating whole nutmeg fresh, as it gives a more vibrant flavor than pre-ground powder.

Is nutmeg safe?

In the small amounts used in everyday cooking, nutmeg is completely safe and has been used for centuries. However, nutmeg contains a natural compound called myristicin, which in very large doses — far beyond anything used in cooking, such as multiple tablespoons — can be toxic. It can cause nausea, vomiting, dizziness, a rapid heartbeat, and even hallucinations. This is not a concern in normal kitchen use, but it is worth knowing that nutmeg should never be consumed in large quantities.

The word nutmeg by itself can also refer to the tree that produces the spice, not just the spice itself. Saying "a nutmeg tree" or simply "a nutmeg" in a botanical or agricultural context refers to this evergreen tropical plant.

In football (soccer), a nutmeg refers to a specific trick move: when one player kicks or passes the ball through an opponent's legs and then collects it on the other side. The ball travels between the opponent's feet while the opponent fails to stop it.

It is considered both a skillful and a somewhat embarrassing move — skillful for the person who does it, and humiliating for the person whose legs the ball goes through. You will hear phrases like "he got nutmegged" (it happened to him) or "she scored after a brilliant nutmeg in midfield."

This meaning is especially common in British English and throughout football culture worldwide.

Less commonly, nutmeg is used to describe a warm, medium reddish-brown color — the color of ground nutmeg powder. You might see this in the context of hair color, paint swatches, or fabric descriptions, where "nutmeg" signals a cozy, earthy brownish tone.

ContextWhat "nutmeg" means
Cooking / spicesA hard seed (or its ground powder) from a tropical tree, used as a warm, sweet spice
Botany / farmingThe tree that produces that spice
Football / soccerA trick move where the ball goes through an opponent's legs
Color / designA warm reddish-brown shade

That covers every major use of the noun nutmeg. The spice is by far the most common meaning you will encounter, but if you are watching football or reading a design catalog, the other meanings are just as real.
11194:
A nutrient is any substance that a living thing — a human, an animal, a plant, or even a microscopic organism — takes in from its surroundings and uses to stay alive, grow, and function properly.

Think of your body as a complex machine. To run, a machine needs two things: fuel to power it, and raw materials to build and repair its parts. Nutrients are exactly that — they are the body's fuel and its building material, all in one category.
The One Idea That Makes It Click

Not everything you eat or drink is a nutrient. What makes a substance a nutrient is that the body actually uses it for a biological purpose — to generate energy, to build or repair cells and tissues, to control chemical reactions, or to carry out other vital jobs. If a substance passes through your body without serving any of these roles, it is not a nutrient.

This is the razor-sharp distinction: a nutrient must be used by the body in some constructive, biological way.

Nutrients are not all the same thing. Scientists group them into categories based on what they do and how much of them the body needs.

1. Macronutrients — needed in large amounts

These are the "big three." They provide the body with energy and the structural material it needs.

Carbohydrates are the body's first and preferred source of energy. When you eat bread, rice, fruits, or pasta, you are consuming carbohydrates. Your body breaks them down into a simple sugar called glucose, which powers your cells.

Proteins are the body's builders and repairers. They are used to make muscles, organs, skin, enzymes (which drive chemical reactions), and hormones (which carry signals around the body). Good sources include meat, fish, eggs, dairy, beans, and lentils.

Fats (also called lipids) serve several purposes: they are a rich, long-lasting source of energy; they make up the walls of every cell in your body; they help you absorb certain vitamins; and they protect your organs. Sources include oils, butter, nuts, seeds, and fatty fish.

2. Micronutrients — needed in small amounts

These do not directly provide energy, but without them, the body cannot work correctly. Even tiny deficiencies can cause serious health problems.

Vitamins are organic compounds (meaning they are carbon-based and made by living things). Each vitamin has specific jobs. For example, Vitamin C helps your immune system fight illness and helps wounds heal. Vitamin D helps your body absorb calcium to keep bones strong. B vitamins help convert food into usable energy.

Minerals are inorganic elements — simple, naturally occurring substances that are not made by living things. Examples include calcium (essential for strong bones and teeth), iron (needed to carry oxygen in your blood), zinc (supports the immune system), and potassium (keeps the heart and muscles working properly). You get minerals by eating foods grown in mineral-rich soil or by drinking water.

3. Water

Water is widely recognized as a nutrient — in fact, one of the most essential ones. It makes up roughly 60% of the human body. It transports all other nutrients through the bloodstream, regulates your body temperature, cushions joints, removes waste, and participates in virtually every chemical reaction in the body. A person can survive weeks without food, but only a few days without water.

4. Dietary Fiber

Fiber is a special type of carbohydrate that the human body cannot fully digest. Yet it is important. It feeds the beneficial bacteria in your gut, helps regulate blood sugar levels, keeps digestion moving, and reduces the risk of certain diseases. It is found in vegetables, fruits, whole grains, and legumes. Some scientists classify it as a nutrient; others treat it as a separate category — but either way, it is an important part of what your body needs.

This is a critical distinction you will encounter frequently.

Essential nutrients are substances the body cannot make on its own — or cannot make in sufficient quantities — so they must come from food, drink, or supplements. All vitamins and minerals are essential. Certain amino acids (the building blocks of proteins) are essential. Certain fatty acids (the building blocks of fats) are also essential. If an essential nutrient is missing from your diet, you will eventually become ill.

Non-essential nutrients are ones the body can produce by itself, even if you do not consume them directly. For example, your body can manufacture some amino acids on its own. Under the right conditions (sufficient sunlight exposure), your skin can produce Vitamin D.

One vital point: "non-essential" does not mean "unimportant." It only means the body has an internal way of producing it. Non-essential nutrients are still actively used by the body and still contribute to health.

For humans and animals, the primary source of nutrients is food and drink. This is why the variety and quality of what you eat matters so much — different foods contain different nutrients, and no single food contains all of them in the right amounts.

For plants, nutrients come from a different set of sources: the soil provides minerals like nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium (which is why farmers use fertilizers to replenish them); water carries dissolved minerals in through the roots; and air provides carbon dioxide, which plants convert into carbohydrates through photosynthesis.

For microorganisms like bacteria and fungi, nutrients are absorbed from their surrounding environment — soil, water, decaying matter, or sometimes the body of another organism.

Nutrients can also be taken in through supplements — pills, powders, or liquids that deliver concentrated amounts of specific nutrients, typically used when diet alone is insufficient.
What Happens When Nutrients Are Missing

When the body does not get enough of a particular nutrient, this is called a nutrient deficiency. The consequences depend on which nutrient is lacking:

A lack of Vitamin C causes scurvy — a disease involving bleeding gums, slow wound healing, and extreme fatigue. A lack of iron causes anemia — a condition where the blood cannot carry enough oxygen, leading to exhaustion and weakness. A lack of Vitamin D causes rickets in children (soft, deformed bones) and bone weakness in adults. A lack of iodine impairs thyroid function and can affect brain development.

This shows that even micronutrients — needed in tiny amounts — are absolutely critical. The body is precise about what it needs.

At a broader level, insufficient nutrients mean the body cannot generate energy, cannot build or repair its own tissues, and cannot regulate its own chemical processes. Sustained nutrient deprivation leads to malnutrition, a serious medical condition.
How the Word Is Used in Sentences

• "Spinach is rich in nutrients, particularly iron, folate, and Vitamin K."
  • "The soil in this region has been depleted of nutrients, making it difficult to grow healthy crops."
  • "Water is a nutrient that people often forget to think about."
  • "A balanced diet ensures that your body receives all the essential nutrients it requires."
  • "The patient was diagnosed with a nutrient deficiency and prescribed iron supplements."
  • "Plants absorb nutrients through their roots from the surrounding soil."
Common Phrases Built Around This Word

Nutrient-rich / nutrient-dense — used to describe a food that provides a high amount of nutrients relative to its calorie content. Broccoli, for example, is nutrient-dense; a plain sugar candy is not.

Nutrient deficiency — the condition of having an insufficient amount of a specific nutrient in the body.

Nutrient absorption — the process by which the body takes nutrients out of digested food and moves them into the bloodstream so they can be used.

Macronutrient / micronutrient — shortened, commonly used forms referring to the large-quantity and small-quantity categories described above.

Soil nutrients — the minerals and organic compounds present in soil that plants extract through their roots.

Nutrient cycle — the movement of nutrients through an ecosystem, from soil to plants to animals and back again through decomposition.

If you ever need to recall what a nutrient is in its simplest form:

A nutrient is a substance that a living organism takes in and uses to produce energy, build and repair itself, or regulate its biological processes.

Everything else — the types, the essential vs. non-essential distinction, the sources, the deficiencies — is an expansion of that single core idea.
11195:
Nutrition is the process by which a living being takes in food, breaks it down, and uses the useful parts of it to survive, grow, stay healthy, and function properly.

Think of your body as a machine. Just as a car needs fuel and oil to run, your body needs food and water to live and work. Nutrition is the entire chain of events — from eating food, to digesting it, to your body putting what it extracts to good use.
The Three Ways the Word Is Used

1. As a process happening inside the body

In this sense, nutrition describes what happens after you eat. Your body breaks food down into tiny chemical substances called nutrients. Once absorbed, these nutrients power everything your body does — breathing, thinking, moving, healing, and growing. So when a doctor says "proper nutrition is important for children," they mean children need to consistently eat the right foods so their bodies can extract the right nutrients to develop well.

2. As a field of science

Nutrition is also the name of an entire scientific discipline — the study of the relationship between food and health. Scientists and healthcare professionals in this field investigate questions like: What do different foods contain? How does the body use various nutrients? What happens when someone lacks a particular nutrient? What diets help prevent disease? So when a university offers a "degree in Nutrition," students are studying food science, human biology, and how diet shapes health.

3. As the nourishing value of food itself

Sometimes "nutrition" simply refers to the beneficial value a food provides to your body. For example, "This meal has excellent nutrition" means the meal is rich in substances that genuinely benefit the body. Conversely, "Junk food offers very little nutrition" means it delivers almost nothing useful, even if it fills you up.
What Are Nutrients? (The Heart of Nutrition)

Since nutrition revolves around nutrients, understanding them is essential. Nutrients are the useful chemical substances that food delivers to your body. They fall into two broad groups:

Macronutrients — needed in large amounts every day:

  • Carbohydrates (sugars and starches) — your body's primary and quickest source of energy.
  • Proteins — used to build and repair muscles, tissues, enzymes, and hormones.
  • Fats — provide long-term energy, protect your organs, and help your body absorb certain vitamins.

Micronutrients — needed in smaller amounts, but equally vital:

  • Vitamins (such as Vitamin C, Vitamin D, and the B vitamins) — support hundreds of different body functions.
  • Minerals (such as calcium, iron, and potassium) — support bone strength, nerve signals, blood health, and more.

Water is also considered an essential nutrient. Your body is mostly water, and water is required for virtually every process that takes place inside you.

Good nutrition means your body is consistently receiving the right balance and adequate amounts of all necessary nutrients. The result is energy, healthy growth, a strong immune system, proper organ function, and long-term wellbeing.

Poor nutrition — clinically called malnutrition — happens in more than one way, which surprises many people:

  • Undernutrition: Not getting enough food or enough of the right nutrients. This leads to weakness, poor growth in children, and increased risk of illness.
  • Overnutrition: Eating too much, especially of unhealthy foods, leading to obesity and diseases like type 2 diabetes and heart disease.
  • Hidden hunger: A person can eat plenty of calories and still be malnourished if their diet consistently lacks key vitamins and minerals. For example, eating mostly white rice and little else might fill the stomach but leave the body deficient in iron, Vitamin C, and other crucial nutrients.

• "The doctor emphasized good nutrition during pregnancy."
  • "She studied nutrition at university and became a registered dietitian."
  • "Junk food is high in calories but low in nutrition."
  • "Plants get their nutrition from sunlight, water, and minerals in the soil."
  • "Always check the nutrition label before buying a packaged food product."

• Nutrient (noun) — a specific substance in food that the body needs. "Iron is an important nutrient."
  • Nutritious (adjective) — describes food that is rich in useful nutrients. "Spinach is highly nutritious."
  • Nutritional (adjective) — relating to nutrition. "I checked the nutritional content of the cereal."
  • Malnutrition (noun) — a state of poor nutrition, whether from too little, too much, or the wrong kinds of food.
  • Dietitian / Nutritionist (nouns) — professionals who specialize in nutrition and guide people on what to eat for health.

If you had to remember just one thing: nutrition is the lifelong process of obtaining and using food in a way that keeps a living body alive, healthy, and functioning well — and it is also the science that studies exactly how that process works.
11196:
"Nutritious" describes food or drink that is rich in nutrients — the substances your body needs to survive, grow, stay healthy, and function properly. Nutrients include things like proteins, vitamins, minerals, healthy fats, carbohydrates, and fiber. When a food contains plenty of these, it earns the label "nutritious."

Think of your body as a complex machine. To keep running well, it does not just need fuel to burn — it needs specific building blocks to repair itself, fight illness, and stay strong. Nutritious food provides exactly those building blocks.

Spinach is nutritious. It contains iron, calcium, vitamins A and C, and fiber — all things your body genuinely needs and uses. A donut, by contrast, is not nutritious. It may taste wonderful and give you a quick burst of energy from sugar, but it contains very few nutrients that your body can actually benefit from in a meaningful way.

"Nutritious" is a gradable adjective, meaning something can be more or less nutritious — it is not a simple yes-or-no quality. Brown rice is more nutritious than white rice because it retains more fiber and minerals. Kale is far more nutritious than iceberg lettuce. A meal made with vegetables, beans, and whole grains could be described as highly nutritious.

Several meanings are easy to confuse with "nutritious," so it is worth being precise about what the word does not mean.

It does not mean "delicious." A food can taste amazing but be completely lacking in nutrients — think of candy or chips. Equally, a food can be highly nutritious without being everyone's favorite in terms of taste.

It does not mean "filling." A food can make your stomach feel full without actually giving your body useful nutrients. Plain white bread may fill you up, but it is not very nutritious.

It does not mean "low-calorie." Some of the most nutritious foods in the world — avocados, nuts, salmon, olive oil — are also high in calories. Calories are simply units of energy. How nutritious a food is depends on what nutrients it contains, not on how many calories it has.

It does not mean "organic." Organic describes how a food was grown — without certain pesticides or synthetic chemicals. A food can be organic but not very nutritious, or deeply nutritious but not organic.

It is not identical to "healthy." These two words are close, but "healthy" is a much broader word. You can describe a person, a lifestyle, a habit, or a mindset as "healthy." "Nutritious" is used almost exclusively for food and drink — specifically to describe whether those foods are rich in the nutrients your body needs. You would say "a healthy person," not "a nutritious person."

Nourishing is the word most similar to "nutritious." Both describe food that gives the body what it needs. The difference is subtle: "nourishing" tends to carry a warmer, more personal or emotional quality — a nourishing bowl of soup feels caring and restorative. "Nutritious" sounds more factual and clinical — it is the word a doctor or nutritionist is more likely to use.

Wholesome is broader than both. It suggests food that is natural, pure, simple, and good in an honest sense. A wholesome meal feels right in a general, moral sort of way; a nutritious meal is specifically about being rich in the nutrients your body needs. These two words often overlap in practice, but they are not the same idea.

"Nutritious" is used almost exclusively with food and drink vocabulary: a nutritious meal, a nutritious diet, a nutritious snack, a nutritious drink, a nutritious recipe, nutritious ingredients. You cannot call a person, a city, a song, or a book "nutritious" in normal, literal usage — those would simply be wrong contexts for this word.

In everyday English, "nutritious" pairs naturally with certain words. You will frequently encounter phrases like highly nutritious, nutritious and delicious, a nutritious diet, a nutritious breakfast, quick and nutritious, and nutritious ingredients. Knowing these natural combinations will help you use and recognize the word confidently.

1. "Eggs are one of the most nutritious foods you can eat — they contain protein, healthy fats, and a wide range of vitamins."
  2. "She always makes sure her children have a nutritious breakfast before school."
  3. "Fast food is rarely nutritious because it tends to be low in vitamins and fiber and high in salt and unhealthy fats."
  4. "The doctor recommended a balanced, nutritious diet to support his recovery."
  5. "These smoothies are both delicious and nutritious."
  6. "Just because something looks natural or green does not automatically mean it is nutritious."
  7. "Lentils are surprisingly nutritious — they are packed with protein, iron, and fiber."

In short: if a food gives your body the substances it genuinely needs to work well and stay healthy, that food is nutritious. The more of those useful nutrients it contains, the more nutritious it is.
11197: When you call something nutritive, you are saying one of two closely related things: either that it provides nourishment to the body, or that it relates to the process of nutrition. Think of it as a word that points to anything connected to feeding, nourishing, or sustaining the body with what it needs.

Your body constantly needs certain substances — proteins, carbohydrates, fats, vitamins, minerals — to grow, repair itself, produce energy, and stay alive. The process of taking in and using those substances is called nutrition. Anything that participates in, supports, or describes that process can be called nutritive.

So nutritive is simply the adjective form of nutrition.
The Two Senses of the Word

Sense 1 — "Nourishing; providing nutrition"

This is the most common everyday use. When you describe food or a substance as nutritive, you mean it contains real, useful nourishment — it gives your body what it actually needs.

"She ate a nutritive meal of vegetables, beans, and whole grains."
"The doctor recommended nutritive broths to help the patient recover."

Here, nutritive means the food is not empty or hollow — it genuinely feeds and sustains you.

Sense 2 — "Of or relating to nutrition" (as a process)

In more scientific or technical writing, nutritive is used to describe things that belong to, or are part of, the process of nutrition itself — not just the food, but the biological machinery involved.

"The body's nutritive processes slow down during sleep."
"Scientists studied the nutritive absorption of minerals in the intestine."

Here, nutritive doesn't describe food — it describes a function, process, or mechanism that is part of how the body nourishes itself.

This is an important distinction. Nutritious and nutritive overlap, but they are not always interchangeable.

Nutritious is the everyday, conversational word. You use it to simply say that food is good for you and full of nutrients.

"Spinach is very nutritious."

Nutritive, on the other hand, is more formal and more versatile. It can mean "nourishing" (just like nutritious), but it can also describe processes, properties, values, and functions related to nutrition — things that nutritious cannot do.

You would say "the nutritive value of an apple" or "nutritive processes in the body," but you would not naturally say "the nutritious value of an apple" or "nutritious processes in the body." In those contexts, only nutritive works.

A simple way to remember this: nutritious is almost always about food being good for you; nutritive is broader and can describe anything tied to the world of nutrition.

Nutritive value — This phrase appears constantly in health, food science, and medicine. It refers to the amount of useful nutrition a food provides. A food with high nutritive value gives you a lot of what your body needs; one with low nutritive value (like plain candy) gives your body very little of use.

"White bread has lower nutritive value than whole-grain bread."

Nutritive sweeteners vs. non-nutritive sweeteners — This is a widely used distinction in food science and nutrition labeling. A nutritive sweetener is one that actually provides calories and energy to the body — like sugar, honey, or corn syrup. A non-nutritive sweetener is one that tastes sweet but provides little to no calories or nutrition — like stevia, aspartame, or saccharin. The word nutritive here is doing exactly what it always does: telling you whether the substance provides genuine nourishment or not.

Nutritive content / nutritive properties — These phrases describe what a food or substance contains in terms of nutrition, or what nutritional qualities it has.

"The nutritive content of this drink includes iron, calcium, and Vitamin D."

Nutritive processes / nutritive functions — Used in biology and medicine to describe the body's internal mechanisms for digesting, absorbing, and using nutrients.

"Researchers examined the nutritive functions of the small intestine."
The Full Picture in One Sentence

Nutritive is a formal adjective that means either "providing nourishment to the body" or "relating to the process of nutrition" — and it is the word you reach for when you want to describe food, substances, processes, or properties through the lens of whether and how they feed and sustain the human body.
11198: A nutter is an informal word — mostly British — for a person who behaves in a crazy, irrational, or wildly eccentric way. When you call someone a nutter, you are saying they think or act in a way that seems completely detached from normal, sensible behavior.

This word is interesting because it sits on a spectrum. The same word can be used in two noticeably different ways depending on the situation:

1. Lovable, harmless crazy
Sometimes "nutter" is used with warmth or even admiration. It describes someone who is delightfully weird, unpredictable, or funny — the kind of person who does things that make you laugh and say, "Only they would do that."

"My uncle wore a Viking helmet to my sister's wedding. He's an absolute nutter, but we love him."

Here, calling him a nutter is almost a compliment. It means he's entertainingly off-beat.

2. Dangerously unhinged
On the other end, "nutter" can describe someone who acts recklessly, aggressively, or frighteningly — a person you would want to stay away from.

"Some nutter started screaming at strangers on the bus for no reason."

Here it's a warning. The person is unpredictable in a way that feels genuinely unsafe.
How to Tell Which Meaning Is Intended

Context is everything. Pay attention to:

  • Tone: A warm, laughing tone → harmless eccentric. A tense, alarmed tone → dangerous/unstable.
  • The action described: Wearing mismatched socks or adopting 12 cats → harmless nutter. Picking fights with strangers or driving recklessly → dangerous nutter.
  • Degree words: "A bit of a nutter" softens it — it means mildly eccentric. "A complete nutter" or "an absolute nutter" intensifies it, though it can go either way.

"Nutter" is primarily British English. You'll hear it constantly in the UK — in casual conversation, on TV, in newspapers. It's also used in Australian and New Zealand English. Americans would understand it but wouldn't naturally use it themselves; they'd be more likely to say "nutjob," "wacko," or "lunatic."
The Sensitive Side of the Word

Historically, "nutter" was sometimes used to describe people with serious mental illness. Today, that usage is considered offensive and stigmatizing by many — it reduces a medical condition to mockery. Most modern, thoughtful speakers use "nutter" only in the lighter, informal sense (eccentric, reckless, wild) and avoid applying it to genuine mental health conditions. If you use this word, be aware of this history.

WordFeel
  • Eccentric — formal, neutral, even elegant. A nutter is informal; an eccentric is what you call them in a newspaper.
  • Weirdo — milder than nutter; it's just about being strange, not necessarily wild or reckless.
  • Lunatic / maniac — stronger, harsher, more clinical in feel. Nutter has a more casual, almost affectionate British energy that these lack.
  • Nutcase — very close in meaning to nutter; used in similar contexts; also informal.

A nutter is an informal British word for a person whose behavior is crazy, irrational, or wildly eccentric — ranging from "hilariously unpredictable" at the softer end, to "frighteningly unhinged" at the sharper end. The exact meaning depends on context and tone. Use it with care, as applying it to mental illness is considered disrespectful.
11199:
To nuzzle means to gently press, push, or rub your nose, snout, or face against someone or something — almost always as an expression of love, affection, or the desire for comfort.

Picture a dog that walks up to you and softly presses its nose into your hand. It isn't biting, it isn't licking — it's just leaning its face into you, warmly and tenderly. That is nuzzling. Or imagine a horse pressing its velvety snout into your palm. That soft, gentle, face-first contact is exactly what this word describes.

Animals do it most naturally and most often — dogs, cats, horses, rabbits, and many others. But humans nuzzle too. A mother might nuzzle her newborn's cheek. Two people in love might nuzzle each other. A sleepy child might nuzzle into a parent's shoulder.

This is never a cold or neutral word. Nuzzle almost always carries warmth. It signals tenderness, closeness, and softness. You would never describe someone nuzzling aggressively — that would completely contradict what the word means. Wherever you see "nuzzle," expect gentleness and affection.

Nuzzle works in two ways:

With a direct object — where something or someone is being nuzzled:

  • "The kitten nuzzled my hand."
  • "She nuzzled the baby's cheek."

With a preposition (usually against or into) — where someone leans or presses toward something:

  • "The child nuzzled against her father's shoulder."
  • "He nuzzled into her neck."

Both forms are very common, so it's worth knowing both.

While nuzzle is most precisely about nose or face contact, it's also used more loosely to mean burrowing or snuggling close to something for warmth or comfort. For example, "She nuzzled into the warm blanket on a cold morning" might not literally mean she rubbed her nose on the blanket — it just paints a picture of her pressing her face cozily into it. This broader, more general use is extremely common in everyday writing.
More examples to lock it in

• "The foal nuzzled its mother, searching for milk."
  • "The puppy nuzzled against the older dog's side and fell asleep."
  • "He nuzzled her hair and told her everything would be okay."
  • "The baby nuzzled into the soft blanket, completely at peace."
  • "She felt the horse nuzzle her palm gently."
The one thing to always remember
Nuzzle = a gentle, loving, face-first press or rub toward a person, animal, or object. Tenderness is inseparable from this word. Every time you encounter it, warmth is being described.
